summary: Kole Jain argues that learning only UI design (styling a landing page or a button) is like decorating a single room, while product design is designing the whole house: the flow, the function, the wiring and how it all connects. He builds product design on three ideas. First, design every state users actually meet (empty, loading, success and error), not just the happy path. Second, build for flow: think in screens and sequences instead of website sections, and ask how the user got to a screen and what they need next. Third, use a design system for clarity, keeping buttons, spacing, type and color consistent so people trust the product and every new screen feels familiar. For someone building a design system, this sets the purpose of the system (trust and speed through consistency, not decoration) and adds state coverage and flow thinking to the checklist for every component and screen.
key_ideas: UI design is decorating one room; product design is designing the whole house, including flow, function and wiring.
Polished visuals alone do not get people hired; a portfolio of products that solve a problem makes landing a job much more likely.
Linear is loved for its clarity (states, flows and system), not only for how it looks.
Most designers design only the happy path, but real apps must handle empty, loading, success and error states.
A thoughtful empty state, like Dub's, has an animation, a message and a clear next step, so users are not left staring at a blank screen.
Giving immediate status after an action (such as a build status after a deploy) keeps users informed and in control.
Design an application in screens and sequences, not in sections the way you would a website.
When building a flow, ask how the user got there and what they need next.
A flow is a chain of tiny decisions, and product design is making those transitions feel natural.
A design system is not just aesthetic; it is how users build trust and speed with the product.
Consistent meaning builds trust: in a macOS pop-up the primary color is always the non-destructive action.
Keeping button spacing, type scales and color scheme consistent makes new screens, such as a new modal, easy to build and familiar to use.
A design system is not about having hundreds of components; it is about making decisions you can stick to.

rules.rule: Design every state a user can meet for each screen and feature (empty, loading, success and error), not only the happy path.
rules.why: Real apps need to handle all the states users actually experience; these tiny moments make or break the experience.
rules.evidence: real apps need to handle all the states users actually experience

rules.rule: Never leave a screen with no data blank; show an empty state with an animation, a message and a clear next step or call to action.
rules.why: Dub's dashboard does this so users are not left staring at a blank screen, and it points them to what to do next (in the hiring tool: start posting job links).
rules.evidence: There's a thoughtful empty state with an animation, a message, and a clear next step

rules.rule: After an action whose result is not instant, such as a deploy, tell the user its status immediately.
rules.why: Users are never left guessing whether it worked; this keeps them informed and in control.
rules.evidence: you get a notification about the build status

rules.rule: When connecting an integration (for example to Notion), show an informative loading state, then either a success message or an error message when it finishes.
rules.why: Applying the same state thinking keeps the user informed during and after the integration.
rules.evidence: we could have an informative loading state and either a success message or an error message

rules.rule: Design an application in screens and sequences, not in sections the way you would design a website.
rules.why: Product design is about the flow, the function and how it all connects, like designing the entire house rather than decorating one room.
rules.evidence: Instead of thinking in sections like you would for a website

rules.rule: For every screen in a flow, ask how the user got there and what they need next.
rules.why: It sounds obvious when looking at a fully built flow, but these questions matter while constructing it; product design is about making the tiny transitions feel natural.
rules.evidence: you need to ask how the user got there and what they need next

rules.rule: After a create step, prompt the natural next step (such as adding members to a new team space) and offer a way to skip, instead of closing everything.
rules.why: A team space is not much without members; Notion's prompt with a skip option is the source's example of a thoughtful user flow.
rules.evidence: they immediately prompt add team members with the option to skip

rules.rule: Keep buttons, spacing and text styles exactly the same across very different contexts, such as a settings panel and a create-view dialog.
rules.why: Consistency gives clarity as products grow more complex and is how users build trust and speed with the product.
rules.evidence: the buttons, spacing, text styles are all exactly the same

rules.rule: Keep what the primary color means the same in every dialog; in macOS pop-ups it always marks the non-destructive action.
rules.why: Users learn the convention and trust that it is always that way, which protects them from mistakes.
rules.evidence: the primary color is the non-destructive action and I trust that it's always that way

rules.rule: Build new screens, such as a new modal, from the components and styles already in the system (button spacing, type scale, color scheme) instead of designing them from scratch.
rules.why: Because spacing on buttons, type scales and color scheme were kept the same throughout, a new modal is super easy to create and every new screen feels familiar even when its content differs.
rules.evidence: every new screen starts to feel familiar, even if the content is different

rules.rule: Don't measure a design system by how many components it has; make decisions you can stick to (such as button spacing, type scale and color scheme) and hold them everywhere.
rules.why: The source says the system is about making decisions you can stick to, not about having hundreds of components; combined with strong flows and real states, that is what turns page design into product building.
rules.evidence: it's not about having hundreds of components

rules.rule: Put products that solve a problem, with their states and flows, in a design portfolio, not only polished landing pages and buttons.
rules.why: No one hires designers just for polished visuals; products that solve a problem make landing a job much more likely.
rules.evidence: put together a portfolio with products that solve a problem

rules.rule: Treat a task as a chain of tiny decisions (for example: contact an applicant, pick an email template, choose whether to add other applicants before sending) and make each transition between them feel natural.
rules.why: That is not just one design but several tiny decisions chained together, and product design is about making these transitions feel natural.
rules.evidence: product design is about making these tiny transitions feel natural

rules.rule: Keep status animations subtle but meaningful.
rules.why: The source lists them among the details that give Linear its clarity, next to hover context and guiding empty states.
rules.evidence: Even the status animations are subtle but meaningful

rules.rule: Show context when the user hovers over an item such as an issue.
rules.why: It is one of the details the source credits for Linear's clarity.
rules.evidence: Hover over an issue, you get context

decisions.question: What should a screen show when there is nothing in it yet?

options.name: A blank screen
options.effect: The user is left staring at an empty screen with no idea what to do.

options.name: A thoughtful empty state
options.effect: An animation, a message and a clear next step or call to action (Dub's dashboard; in the hiring tool, a prompt to start posting job links).
options.when: Any list, dashboard or area that can be empty, such as no hires to manage.

decisions.recommendation: Use a thoughtful empty state with an animation, a message and a clear next step, because it guides users instead of leaving them facing a blank screen.
decisions.evidence: it doesn't leave you staring at a blank screen

decisions.question: How should the product report the result of an action that takes time, like a deploy or connecting an integration?

options.name: No status
options.effect: Users are left guessing whether it worked.

options.name: Loading state, then success or error
options.effect: An informative loading state while it runs, then a success message or an error message (or an immediate build status notification, as in Vercel).
options.when: Deploys, integrations and other actions whose outcome is not instant.

decisions.recommendation: Show an informative loading state and then a clear success or error message, because it keeps users informed and in control.
decisions.evidence: informative loading state and either a success message or an error message

decisions.question: Should you structure the product like a website or like an application?

options.name: Sections, like a website
options.effect: Each part is designed as a standalone section or page.
options.when: The source associates this with websites.

options.name: Screens and sequences, like an application
options.effect: Each screen is designed as a step, with attention to how the user arrived and what they need next.

decisions.recommendation: Think in screens and sequences for applications, asking how the user got there and what they need next.
decisions.evidence: think in screens and sequences like you would for a real application

decisions.question: When a user finishes creating something, should the flow end or lead them onward?

options.name: Close everything on create
options.effect: The task ends; the new item may be incomplete, like a team space with no members.
options.when: The source mentions it only as what Notion could have done.

options.name: Prompt the next step, with a skip option
options.effect: The user is led straight into the natural next task (add team members) but can skip it.
options.when: When the created item is not much use without a follow-up step.

decisions.recommendation: Prompt the natural next step with an option to skip; the source calls Notion's version a thoughtful user flow.
decisions.evidence: Notion could have just closed everything once they hit create

decisions.question: What makes a design system worth having: many components, or a few decisions held consistently?

options.name: Hundreds of components
options.effect: A large library; the source says this is not what the system is about.

options.name: A few decisions you stick to
options.effect: Button spacing, type scales and color scheme stay the same everywhere, so new screens feel familiar and users build trust and speed.
options.when: Always, and more so as the product gets more complex.

decisions.recommendation: Make decisions you can stick to and keep them consistent across every context, because clarity and trust come from consistency, not component count.
decisions.evidence: It's about making a decision. you can stick to

decisions.question: In a confirmation pop-up, which action should carry the primary color?

options.name: The non-destructive action
options.effect: The primary-colored button is always the safe choice, so users learn to trust it (the macOS convention the presenter says has saved him many times).
options.when: Confirmation pop-ups that offer a destructive and a non-destructive action.

options.name: Whichever action the screen wants to push
options.effect: The meaning of the primary color changes from dialog to dialog, so users cannot rely on it.
options.when: The source never recommends it; it is the opposite of the consistency it praises [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Give the primary color to the non-destructive action and keep it that way everywhere, because users trust a convention that never changes.
decisions.evidence: the primary color is the non-destructive action and I trust that it's always that way

process.step: Go past UI into product design
process.detail: Move from styling single screens (a landing page, a button, a portfolio) to designing the flow, function and connections of a whole product that solves a problem.
For each feature, design beyond the happy path: empty states with a message and next step, informative loading states, and success or error messages when an action finishes.

Think in screens and sequences; for each screen ask how the user got there and what they need next, and chain the tiny decisions so transitions feel natural (for example: click to contact an applicant, pick an email template, then choose whether to add other applicants before sending).
Pull out components and keep button spacing, type scales and color scheme the same everywhere, so new screens such as a modal are quick to assemble and feel familiar.
Hold to the decisions you made rather than growing hundreds of components; combined with strong flows and real states, this turns page design into product building.

caveats: Sponsor segment for Dualite Alpha (Figma link to a working web app 'in under 2 minutes', a 38% discount code, and the hiring dashboard files hosted there); it is also plugged in the description and excluded from rules.
Career-advice framing: statements about who gets hired are the presenter's opinion, not data. The transcript says 'in 2025' while the description says 'in 2026'.
No exact values are given: no spacing, type sizes, colors, durations or animation settings, so the rules are qualitative. The on-screen Figma examples are not described in detail in the transcript.

Auto-caption errors: 'Dual Light Alpha' is Dualite Alpha (the description links dualite.dev) and 'Versell' is Vercel [inferred]; 'real estates' near the end likely means 'real states' and 'no hier to manage' likely means 'no hires to manage' [inferred].
The macOS pop-up example is a personal observation of one convention; the video does not say what the primary color should mark in other platforms or products.
